questions.title: Enveloped viruses exit by budding or exocytosis
questions.question: How do enveloped viruses exit their host?

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Rupturing the virus" describes destroying the virion, not the mechanism by which an intact enveloped virus leaves the host cell.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bursting (lysing) the host cell is instead the typical exit route for many naked (non-enveloped) viruses, which lack an envelope to bud through.
explanations.C: Correct. Enveloped viruses exit the host cell by budding through the host's plasma or nuclear membrane (or via exocytosis), acquiring their lipid envelope from that host membrane in the same process. The viral envelope is lipoprotein in nature; its lipid portion is acquired from the host cell's plasma or nuclear membrane during the budding process, while its protein portion is coded by the viral genome. This exit route lets the host cell often survive and continue producing virus, unlike the lytic exit typical of many naked viruses.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Budding or exocytosis" correctly describes enveloped-virus exit, so "none of these" is wrong.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Endocytosis is a mechanism of viral ENTRY into a host cell, not exit from one.

questions.learning_objective: State that enveloped viruses exit the host cell by budding or exocytosis, acquiring their envelope from the host membrane.

questions.title: Latent viral infection: occult, reactivating form
questions.question: What is a latent viral infection?

options.A: The virus initially presents with symptoms but then hides until it can be active and produce symptoms
options.C: Infection develops rapidly but lasts for a short time
options.D: Slow development, reactions to disease are less severe, likely to be present for a long time

explanations.A: Correct. A latent viral infection is one in which the virus persists in an occult (hidden, non-productive) form inside the infected cell after the initial infection, later reactivating to produce symptoms again -- classic examples include herpes simplex and varicella-zoster virus reactivation. This occult, reactivating pattern is distinct from a chronic infection (ongoing, detectable low-level replication throughout) or a slow infection (long incubation, progressive disease with no true dormancy). Latency lets the virus persist in the body indefinitely, evading full immune clearance between reactivation episodes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Option A correctly describes latent infection, so "none of the above" is wrong.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Rapid development with a short overall duration describes an acute infection, not a latent one, which by definition persists for the long term with intervening dormancy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Slow, progressive development with milder but long-lasting reactions describes a slow virus infection (for example subacute sclerosing panencephalitis), a different persistence pattern from latency's occult-then-reactivating course.

questions.learning_objective: Define latent viral infection as an occult, reactivating form of persistence, distinct from chronic or slow infection.

questions.title: First line of defense against viral infection: interferon
questions.question: First Line of Defense against viral infection is?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A general inflammatory response is a broader, slower-acting host reaction, not the specific rapid antiviral defense targeted here.
explanations.B: Correct. Type I interferons (IFN-alpha and IFN-beta) are produced early in the course of a viral infection, chiefly by virally infected cells themselves and by plasmacytoid dendritic cells, and act on neighbouring, still-uninfected cells to induce an intracellular antiviral state that slows the infection's spread. This rapid, non-specific innate response occurs well before the adaptive immune system (antibodies, cytotoxic T cells) has time to mount a specific response, making it the genuine first line of defense against viral infection. Type I interferon also increases NK-cell activity, adding a second early antiviral effect.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Type I interferon correctly answers this question, so "none of the above" is wrong.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cell-mediated immunity (cytotoxic T cells) is an adaptive response that takes days to develop after antigen presentation, acting later than the immediate interferon response, not as the first line of defense.

questions.learning_objective: State that type I interferon, produced early by infected cells, is the first line of defense against viral infection.

questions.title: Virus in the bloodstream is viraemia
questions.question: Presence of viruses in the blood stream is known as?

explanations.A: Correct. Viraemia is the presence of virus particles in the bloodstream, the hallmark of a systemic viral infection -- a systemic infection is characterized by viraemia, involvement of multiple organs and, typically, long-lasting immunity after recovery, unlike a localized infection, which multiplies only at the entry site with no severe viraemia. Viraemia can be primary (from the initial entry site) or secondary (from replication in a deeper organ, seeding further spread), and it is what allows a systemically spreading virus to reach distant target organs.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bacteraemia is the presence of bacteria in the bloodstream, the bacterial (not viral) equivalent of this term.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Septicaemia describes a systemic illness caused by bacteria (or their toxins) multiplying in the blood, a bacterial clinical syndrome, not the general term for virus in blood.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pyemia describes pus-forming bacteria spreading via the bloodstream to seed abscesses, an unrelated bacterial term.

questions.learning_objective: State that viraemia is the presence of virus in the bloodstream, characteristic of systemic viral infection.

questions.title: Capsid is the protein coat around the nucleic acid
questions.question: The protein coat which surrounds the nucleic acid of animal viruses is called?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The envelope is an additional, outer lipid layer found only in enveloped viruses, surrounding the nucleocapsid -- it is not itself the protein coat directly around the nucleic acid.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The nucleocapsid is the nucleic acid PLUS the capsid together, not the protein coat alone; describing it as just "the protein coat" omits the enclosed nucleic acid it also names.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A capsomer is only one individual small protein subunit that assembles, together with many others, into the complete capsid -- not the whole protein coat itself.
explanations.D: Correct. The capsid (nucleocapsid) is the structural component found in all viruses -- the protein coat surrounding the viral genome, together forming the nucleocapsid. Its functions include protecting the viral genome, mediating attachment to host-cell receptors, and conferring antigenicity, but it does NOT confer sensitivity to 70% alcohol, a property instead associated with the lipid envelope. This is the one structural component every virus has, enveloped or not, distinguishing it from the envelope (present only in some viruses) or a fixed nucleic acid type.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the capsid as the protein coat surrounding the nucleic acid of a virus.

questions.title: Viroid: circular RNA, no protein or envelope
questions.question: Viroids are?

options.A: Viruses are genetically deficient and so incapable of producing Infection's daughter virion
options.B: Infective agents with low molecular weight RNA and no proteins
options.C: Protein infections particles, lack detectable nucleic acid

explanations.A: Incorrect. This describes a defective virus (a genetically deficient virus unable to produce infectious daughter virions independently), a different infectious agent from a viroid.
explanations.B: Correct. A viroid is defined as a small, circular RNA molecule lacking both an envelope and a protein coat (capsid) -- an infective agent with low-molecular-weight RNA and no proteins, exactly as this option states. This distinguishes it from a satellite virus (which needs a helper virus to replicate) or a prion (an infectious protein with no nucleic acid at all, the opposite composition). Viroids are classically associated with plant diseases, not human infection.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This describes a prion (protein-only, no detectable nucleic acid), the exact opposite composition of a viroid, which is RNA-only with no protein.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Extrachromosomal genetic elements" describes a plasmid, a DNA element unrelated to a viroid's uncoated circular RNA composition.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A viroid's genome is RNA, not DNA, so it cannot be classed among DNA viruses; it is also not a true virus at all, lacking a capsid.

questions.learning_objective: Define a viroid as a circular RNA molecule without an envelope or protein coat.

questions.title: Enveloped viruses obtain envelope by budding
questions.question: Enveloped viruses obtain their envelopes by?

options.A: Modifying vesicles that may be used in the exporting of cellular proteins
options.B: Breaking down the membrane of the cell they infect and incorporating the lipid into the capsids
options.C: Budding through the cells or nuclear membrane as they leave the infected cell
options.D: Encoding an enzyme which synthesizes the necessary lipids for the envelope

explanations.A: Incorrect. Modifying secretory-pathway vesicles is not the standard, general mechanism taught for how enveloped viruses acquire their envelope; the general rule is budding through a host membrane.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Enveloped viruses do not break down and destroy the host membrane; instead they bud through it intact, incorporating a portion of it as their own envelope while the host cell can often survive.
explanations.C: Correct. The viral envelope is lipoprotein in nature; its lipid portion is acquired from the host cell's plasma or nuclear membrane during the budding process, while its protein portion is coded by the viral genome. Budding through the cell's plasma membrane or nuclear membrane as the virion leaves the infected cell is the general mechanism by which enveloped viruses obtain their envelope. This is also, correspondingly, the general mechanism by which enveloped viruses exit the host cell.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A virus does not encode an enzyme to synthesize new lipids from scratch for its envelope; it instead acquires ready-made host membrane lipid during budding.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Since A, B and D are each individually incorrect, "all of the above" cannot be correct.

questions.learning_objective: State that enveloped viruses obtain their envelope by budding through the host cell's plasma or nuclear membrane.

questions.title: Envelope structures: lipoproteins
questions.question: The envelope surrounding the nucleocapsid of some viruses is made up of which of the following structures?

explanations.A: Correct. The viral envelope is lipoprotein in nature; its lipid portion is acquired from the host cell's plasma or nuclear membrane during the budding process, while its protein portion (the glycoprotein spikes) is coded by the viral genome. This lipoprotein composition is what makes the envelope sensitive to detergents and lipid solvents, which dissolve its lipid component. It is a structure found only in enveloped viruses -- naked viruses lack it entirely.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) is a component of the Gram-negative bacterial outer membrane, not the viral envelope.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Peptidoglycan is the bacterial cell-wall polymer, not a component of the viral envelope.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chitin is a fungal cell-wall polysaccharide, not a component of the viral envelope.

questions.learning_objective: State that the viral envelope is composed of lipoprotein.

questions.title: Capsid is found in all viruses
questions.question: Structural component that is found in all viruses is?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The envelope is present only in enveloped viruses; naked viruses have no envelope at all, so it is not universal.
explanations.B: Incorrect. DNA is only the genome type of DNA viruses; RNA viruses instead carry RNA, so a fixed nucleic acid type is not shared by all viruses.
explanations.C: Correct. The capsid (nucleocapsid) is the structural component found in all viruses -- enveloped or not -- unlike envelope, spikes, or a fixed nucleic acid type. Its functions include protecting the viral genome, mediating attachment to host-cell receptors, and conferring antigenicity. This universality is what makes the capsid, not the envelope or genome type, the one truly common structural feature across every virus family.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Tail fibers are a structure specific to certain bacteriophages (for example T4 phage), not a component found in all viruses generally.

questions.learning_objective: State that the capsid is the one structural component found in all viruses.
